utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there was a brief preliminary matter to be raised before we start.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. After meeting with the witness in preparation for her testimony, the Prosecution is seeking to redact two sentences from her proposed 92 ter statement, and these sentences are in paragraph 9 of her statement. The Prosecution will not be relying on these sentences as part of her evidence. This redacted version has been uploaded into e-court with the same 65 ter number as the original statement, and it also has been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now the Chamber is wondering which two sentences you are not relying on. If you could say the -- perhaps just the first few words. You said it was in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In paragraph 9. We have no paragraphs on the version which is attached to the 92 ter motion, but I do understand from one of my colleagues that it is the paragraph starting with: "When I was in Potocari, I saw."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours. And the new version also has numbers that has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So I will begin the sentence where the redaction starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: "I was there when Mladic said," and the redaction continues through, "I also heard when the males were killed." Does that explain the two sentences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we continue where it was, "I was on the right side."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that where we restart, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That is clear. If there's nothing else, then the Chamber can be brought into the courtroom -- the witness can be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at the Bench, you'll see who is speaking to you at this moment. I am speaking to you. Witness, before you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- give evidence, you are required to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is handed out to you. I do understand that you can read. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Osmanovic, we'll start your examination by the Prosecution. The Prosecution will first examine you, and Ms. MacGregor will put the questions to you, and you'll find Ms. MacGregor to your right, close to you. Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Could I please ask that 65 ter 28891, the English version of this document, be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Ms. Osmanovic, I've asked for a document to be loaded onto your screen in front of you, and while that is loading, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2000 about what happened to you during and after the war?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yesterday, was your statement read to you in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, if you can please look at the first page of the document that's in front of you. The English version on the bottom right-hand side, are you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do. It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Does that statement reflect the answers that you gave during that interview?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And was the statement true to the best of your knowledge when you gave it?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Would you give the same answers in substance if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why wouldn't I? Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we move for the admission of this statement as this witness's Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1461, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1461 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now read a short summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained to the witness that it is -- what the purpose of it is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please be patient, Ms. Osmanovic. The summary of your testimony will be read now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Saliha Osmanovic is a Bosnian Muslim who lived in Dobrak in the municipality of Srebrenica when the war broke out. In May 1992, Mrs. Osmanovic fled to the town of Srebrenica where she lived with her husband and two sons until the town fell in July 1995. On 6 July, Mrs. Osmanovic's youngest son, Edin, who was 17, was killed by a VRS shell. On 11 July, Mrs. Osmanovic's other son Nermin who was 18 and her husband Ramo fled through the woods toward free territory. She never saw them again. Fourteen years later, she learned that their remains were found. On 11 July Ms. Osmanovic fled to Potocari. In Potocari she saw General Mladic taking to the crowds of refugees. After spending one night there, Mrs. Osmanovic was directed to board a truck. The men, including her father-in-law, were separated from the women and some were taken to an unfinished house along the road. The remains of Mrs. Osmanovic's father-in-law were eventually found. Mrs. Osmanovic and other prisoners, mostly women, were taken to Tisca and walked to free territory. Since the war, Ms. Osmanovic has lived in many locations. She relies on state assistance provided as compensation for her missing family members. She does not receive a pension for her husband. Since the war she has lived alone and feels she has lost everything that matters. Your Honours, that concludes my summary. May I now proceed with the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may, but let me first address the witness very briefly. Mrs. Osmanovic, I do understand that hearing the summary of your statement to be read to you is emotional for you. If at any point in time you need a short break or you want to just drink a bit of water, don't hesitate to ask me time for that. So as long as you feel sufficiently strong to continue, we'll do so. If you feel that you need a short break or that you are in need of anything else, tell me as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ms. MacGregor will now put the questions to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mrs. Osmanovic, in your statement from 2000 - and that's at paragraph 7, Your Honours - you say that your husband Ramo and son Nermin left when Srebrenica fell to try to walk through the woods to safety. Did Ramo's cousin Kemal Osmanovic go with the men in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I do believe the witness answered but I didn't hear a translation and I don't see one on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we check the microphone is close enough to the witness. Could you please repeat your answer to the question your -- the question was: Did Ramo's cousin Kemal Osmanovic go with the men in the woods? Did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They left together to the forest. I received information that they were seen in the forest, but I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Kemal tell you about being with Ramo and Nermin in the woods?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He did tell me after all of it that he did see him and that Ramo went ahead to see where they would go through. However, he was caught. I don't know what ensued. I wasn't in the forest. I was in Potocari. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did Kemal tell you about when Ramo and Nermin last spoke to each other in the woods?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on 13th. Kemal said he saw Ramo on the 13th and that he talked to him in the forest. It was in the forest, not on a meadow. As I told you, we had separated and I don't know what followed. He said he just went to do some scouting to see where they would go through and then Ramo was caught, as well as the others, and killed. They're gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play a clip from the Srebrenica trial video, and this is Exhibit P00147. Excuse me for a moment. Pardon, Your Honours, P01147. And the clip starts at minute 18. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mrs. Osmanovic, if you can watch the video on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I need to correct the transcript. It begins at minute -- 18 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the clip has an ended at 18 minutes and 57 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mrs. Osmanovic, do you recognise the man that's featured in that video?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I do. This is my man. He was calling out our son Nermin and the others to come down, as I've explained, when he went ahead to look for a way through. That's what I know. This is it. So he's saying, "All of you, come." It was no genocide. It was horror.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In 2000, when you originally gave your statement, you did not know what had happened to Ramo and Nermin. Did you ever find out what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you able to bury their remains?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And for the 14 years that they were missing, did you know anything about what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I watched TV, and I read it for the first time in the newspapers, and I saw my man. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you talking about the video just now?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And while they were missing, did you hold out any hope that they might be alive?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was hoping. I couldn't imagine things would turn out this way. I couldn't believe it. My husband used to work in Belgrade, and we had family friends. What happened, happened. The whole world can see. That's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 8, you state that you went to Potocari on 11 July. Did you go to Potocari from the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And how much time did you have to prepare to leave your house in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't reside in Srebrenica but in Dobrak, in my house. However, I was a tenant in Srebrenica. We were expelled on the 8th of May and went to Srebrenica in 1992, where we stayed until 1995. We simply ran out of our house and set out. What preparation? They said, "Potocari, good luck."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And when you say "they" --

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No preparation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When you say, "They said 'Potocari,'" who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they did. Mladic. Mladic said Bratunac, Potocari. I didn't even know this Mladic. He said straight to Bratunac and Potocari, but my municipality's Bratunac. I married in Srebrenica. I thought there would be another round of slaughter at the stadium in Bratunac when we were stopped in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And when you say that Mladic said to go to Bratunac and Potocari, are you referring to a video you've seen of him in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Have you seen a video --

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Potocari, that's when he said it. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, up until the moment that you boarded the bus in Potocari, do you feel like you could have stayed in Srebrenica if you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Stay? Where? We were in hell. There was hell when the Serb army came in. I knew some of them. I knew a teacher from Bratunac. There was chaos. How could we stay when we were being told to pack up? Mladic said, "Go to Bratunac, and whatever possessions you had, leave it." I was close to him. Not all of the witnesses could come close. He said the Serb army would come in. He distributed some chocolates to the children, and he spilled some water and gave to the people. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In your statement, at paragraph 10, you say that your father-in-law was separated from you in Potocari and taken to an unfinished house. Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. And not only with him. They were being separated on the left-hand [Realtime transcript read in error "right-hand] side to the house. I know the host of that house, and we were on the other side, and we went to first Bratunac and then Tisca. We were separated. I can't even describe what happened. It happened as it did. He's gone. Many people are. Now, what happened there and who separated, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think -- the translation I heard was "left-hand side" and I see that the transcript says "right-hand side." So I'm not sure if I heard correctly or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be -- the transcript will be verified on the basis of the audio, Ms. MacGregor, and special attention will be paid to this portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless one of the parties considers it at this moment of such relevance that it should be clarified immediately. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were the remains of your father-in-law ever found?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And when you gave your statement in 2000, you were living in a house that your brother had bought for you. Do you leave there now?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I returned to my house in Dobrak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And do you live with anyone?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I live alone in my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Have you lived alone since Ramo and Nermin left through the woods?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have lived alone, yes. Well, there were some people around who had been driven out, but I have -- I used to live in my brother's house alone as I do now in my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And how are you able to support yourself financially?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's okay. I receive some disability pension. All in all, it's good, as long as it's not in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Have you ever been employed in your life?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was a housewife. My husband worked, and I tended to the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no additional questions for the witness, and I also will not be offering any other associated exhibits through the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. MacGregor. Before you start your cross-examination, I would have one additional question for the witness. Ms. Osmanovic, you told us that you knew that chocolates were distributed, as you said, by Mr. Mladic, and water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- you said you knew that. You knew that for sure. Did you see that yourself, and did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it with my own pair of eyes. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So did you see it when you were there at the time, or did you see it on a video at any later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Potocari, that's where I saw it. It can't be in the footage, as if I saw the footage and then came to tell you this. I saw him in Potocari. He said, "Whatever possessions you had, discard of those, and the Serb army's going to come in." That's true. I saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Ms. Osmanovic, you'll now be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find Mr. Ivetic to your left, standing there, and Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, I will try to conclude my examination as briefly as possible, and I would only ask you to pay attention to my questions --

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will only ask you to pay attention --

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's begin. Now, first of all, I'd like to ask you in relation to your Rule 92 ter statement, and it's page --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's P1461, and it will be page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S, and the paragraph that is marked with the number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, madam, in this part of your statement, you discuss how your husband and son left and tried to walk to safety with other men through the woods. What I want to know is if you saw them when they left so as to know their appearance and what they took with them.

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On that occasion when they left, did --

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: What would they carry with them? They just left as they were on that occasion. They went to Kazani. It was the place called there [as interpreted]. They fled Srebrenica in 1992. They were not able to carry anything with them, either food or anything. Why would they?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, the question I have for you is on the occasion when they left, did either your husband or your son have in their possession any weapons or explosives?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. How -- how would that be possible? Weapons and explosives in Srebrenica? Everything was confiscated. UNPROFOR is the best placed to tell you what the people in Srebrenica had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am, and we have had evidence from UNPROFOR. I'd like to focus now on what you know.

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm glad of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who made the decision that the males were supposed to go to the woods while the females and children were to go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: How can I know that? I was not a person in charge. I was not a commander. How could I know that? I don't know. Why are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, earlier --

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There were people in Potocari as well, young people. It was hell. People scattered in all directions. They were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, today in the direct examination conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor, at temporary transcript pages 9 through 10, you were asked about the preparations you had before leaving the residence in Srebrenica for Potocari, and you told them they told you to go to Potocari, good luck, and now you've identified that you claim Mr. Mladic is the one that said to go to Potocari. Is that your testimony, or did someone else in Srebrenica advise you to go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a lady, but Mladic didn't tell us to leave Srebrenica, because Srebrenica had been shelling. There's a difference between Srebrenica and Potocari, the town. That's what I said. I know what I said. Mladic told us that in Potocari on the 12th, when the whole group of people was there. He didn't tell us anything in Srebrenica. And you know, it was chaos and hell in Srebrenica. There was shelling. There were aircraft. It was hellish. So it was possible [as interpreted] for Mladic to tell us that in Srebrenica because nobody knew what they would do or what they would -- where they would go. I know what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, for the clarification of when and where you encountered Mr. Mladic. I'd like to focus on the time period before you left for Potocari, and again I'd like to ask you what was the -- did anyone tell you to go to Potocari, and, if so, who?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: You know, when people set off, you don't know where you're going, to which side. Just like if somebody started shooting here, I would join the people and go with the crowd. There was no one who could tell us anything. It was hell. There were shells. We were close to Serbia, Skelani. I cannot say that I saw my neighbours in Potocari, but I did see Mladic, believe me. I know that. I'm not a fool. If I had seen some of my neighbours, I would tell you, I saw this and this person. But there was shooting coming from Serbia. Serbia committed genocide. What's the use of their apology now? What use is the apology? I lost my husband. I lost my sons. I don't need these kind of stories anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Osmanovic, it's me now again who's addressing you. Look just in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Mr. Ivetic would like to know is a few details which he needs to know. Could I first ask you, you said you left from Srebrenica to Potocari. Now, who -- did you leave from your house -- did you leave from your house, and did you then walk to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that after shelling had started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 8th of May, we were at our house. Serbia and Bosnia are divided by the Drina, and the shooting started. My husband used to work in Belgrade for a company that had projects in Algeria and other places. He was in Belgrade, but he came home, and he was supposed to go back in his car. We were simply at home without being aware of what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. You said shooting had started. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- who did leave your home first, you or your husband with your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the last who left. My children left, my husband and Nermin. They went to the woods. I stayed behind, but then we rejoined in the forest across the hill. I was in some villages over there, and then we went to Srebrenica. We were in Srebrenica, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be some confusion about the time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, Ms. Osmanovic, I am focusing on the last day before you went to Potocari where you said you saw Mr. Mladic. Now, you had been living for a few years in Srebrenica, or at least in a village in Srebrenica, if I understand you well. Now, when you last saw your husband, was that when he left your home where you had been residing for quite some time? Was it there that you saw him for the last time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We set off from Srebrenica. I lived in Srebrenica in Veselin's house. My husband and my two sons, that's where we lived in Srebrenica. They headed off towards Kazani. One of my sons was killed on the 6th of July, and then on the 11th of July they set off from Srebrenica. There were thousands of people, and that is when I saw Mladic in Srebrenica. No, I apologise. Not in Srebrenica, in Potocari. That was on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there for a second. When your husband and your son left, as you said, for Kazani, when did you see them for the last time? Was that when they left home or was that at any other moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We left the house all together and then we separated on the 11th. They went to the woods and I to Potocari, and I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there again. You said you left home together. Who decided that you would leave your home? Was it your husband who said, "Let's go," or what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't the only person who left Srebrenica. Thousands left Srebrenica. Those who stayed behind disappeared. Who was to decide that? Who did you expect to tell you anything? You -- you had to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you decided to leave home together, and you joined a large group of people. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there came a moment where your husband and your son went in a different direction from where you went. Do you remember when exactly and where exactly your husband and son separated from you? Was that in Srebrenica? Was that on -- wherever it was. Could you tell us, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in Srebrenica, up there in Srebrenica, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, what did your husband tell you when he separated with your son from you? Did he -- what did he say, or did he say anything, anything at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He told me to go with the other people, because my son, who was killed on the 6th of July, was buried in Kazan, and when Srebrenica fell he just told me, "Go with the other people and see what happens." That's the last thing that he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he went in that other direction, or did you understand that he wanted to go in the direction of the grave of your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you what was happening at that specific moment, what happened. I don't know. I joined the crowd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And your husband did not explain why he separated from you at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I tried to explore some of the elements I think you had on your mind you wanted to explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now continue. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, at the time that your husband and son left through the woods on 11th July 1995, with the other males, was your husband still a member of Ibro's brigade of the Army of BiH in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us, for those of us that are not from Srebrenica, who was this Ibro?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard of Ibro, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was your husband an officer or was he an ordinary soldier?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take a moment to focus on the months leading up to 11th July 1995. During that time period, was your husband spending time with you or was he spending time with Ibro's brigade, or was he spending time with both? If you could explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think if you listen carefully to the witness, she explained, I think, from -- what her husband did. So just to give two options seems not to be the right thing. Could you tell us what your husband did in the month before the take-over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was in the army. He was both at home and in the army. I can't say contrary to that because that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, during the time period in the month leading up to 11 July 1995, when your husband was in the army, was he wearing a military uniform or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea. I know that he left the house in blue jeans, but I didn't follow him in order to see what kind of clothes he would be putting on. I was just a housewife.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, madam, I also have to ask you in relation to your sons. Were either of them also members of the Army of BiH in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Why would children be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in addition to your husband and your son Nermin, am I correct that your two brothers, Salko and Safet, also went with the column of men from Srebrenica through the forest?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, they did. My brother Safet was searched for and found, and Safet [as interpreted] went through the woods and left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you, madam, with respect to your brothers, were either of them part of the Army of BiH in Srebrenica prior to 11 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They were not close to me. I was in the house. There were shells. I didn't venture out. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: If they were, though, they had to defend themselves, because Serbia was armed. They had weapons. We had nothing. That's why we were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, I promised I would have my cross-examination as briefly as possible. The only way we can accomplish that, if you please try to focus on my questions and have your answers be focused on the questions that I've asked. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please, ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to Salko, am I correct that he was among those that successfully broke through the Serb lines to reach Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, successfully, because he had been expelled from his native place of Zaluzje. They wanted to kill him, but he was saved by a Serb, and he drove him all the way to Tuzla, put him on a bus and drove him to Tuzla. And after that he arrived in Srebrenica through the forest, and then Srebrenica fell, and he headed off for Zepa, my brother Salko, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I even know the man who saved him. He was a bus driver on the line servicing between Srebrenica and Bratunac. My brother was wounded in Srebrenica. He was not in the army. I shoot at you, you shoot at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, now I'm confused, madam. Earlier you said with respect to your brothers that you did not know whether they were in the army or not, and now you're saying that your brother Salko was not in the army. Could you please clarify for us.

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he was in the army. I know that he had been expelled from his village. That's what I told you. And I told you that his Serb colleague saved his life and drove him off to Tuzla, and he prevented his being killed. Then he went to Zepa, and two months later he came to Srebrenica. And even if he was in the army, so what? One must live.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, we're just trying to get to the truth and the only way we can do that is by asking questions and receiving answers. So I apologise if you are confused by my questions, but I'm just trying to clarify the details so that we have the full, complete picture. Could you tell us the name of the driver that you say saved your brother?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know any names. I've forgotten the names. I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Madam, Kemo Osmanovic, your cousin, am incorrect that he, too, was a member of the column of men that left for the forest on 11 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He told me, when I saw him after having crossed to the territory in Tuzla, that he saw them in the woods, that Ramo wanted to try and find a way out. That's what he told me. I don't know if they were together and what was going on there. I don't know what was happening up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As to your cousin Kemo, do you know whether he had previously been a member of the Army of BiH in Srebrenica at the time that they set out on 11 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, madam, now I'd like to move briefly to another topic. I want to ask you about the situation in the enclave of Srebrenica in the months leading up to July 1995. With relation to the humanitarian aid that was coming in, am I correct that the same was being offered for sale on the black market by the Bosnian Muslim authorities of the army and civilian government?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I have no knowledge about that. I have no idea. The trucks with food were coming, but the trucks were sent back at the Yellow Bridge, and whether they brought anything in, I don't know, and what happened with that. I don't know. I didn't become involved in politics. I don't need politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask one clarification. You said the trucks were sent back at the Yellow Bridge. Is that what you heard, or is that what you saw yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that. People were telling that trucks full of food were sent back. I only heard of that. I wasn't able to see that. I cannot see either the Yellow Bridge or the trucks from my place in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one further question on this topic before moving on, madam. Did you have any personal knowledge or did you hear from others ever about the existence of a black market in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm hearing of it just now. I don't know what that is. What's a black market? Can you please explain to me in a different way? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, in view of the answer of the witness, there maybe better sources of evidence to explore the black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move now back to your 92 ter statement and it's paragraph 10 on page 3 in both languages. And this -- this is the paragraph where you talk about an encounter with General Mladic and when he said that first the women and children could go and you all moved towards the buses and trucks. And I have to ask you: How close were you to Mladic on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 5 or 10 metres. Let's say 10 metres. I was close enough, because it wasn't possible for everyone to come close to Mladic. There were thousands of people who were unable to see or hear him but I was able.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this encounter that is described in this paragraph of your Rule 92 ter statement, was this the first encounter that you had with General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that that would have been, therefore, on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I saw him on the 12th, and I left Srebrenica on a truck in the evening, and we went to Tisca. At least that's what we were told. I thought that we were going to Bratunac. Mladic said, "You will be completely safe," but I was in such a stress and fear that I didn't hear clearly, but on the way we encountered their army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you say that you left Srebrenica on a truck in the evening. Did the encounter with General Mladic occur in the evening or during the day time?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was daytime on the 12th. There was chocolate. They were distributing chocolates and water to the people. I know that. And I boarded the truck towards the evening. Not only me. We were loaded group by group. Some people were separated to the left, some to the right, on the way to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was about to go to a video-clip of about a minute in length. I see the time. We could also have a break now. It's up to Your Honours how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time do you think in total you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Approximately 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10 to 15 minutes. I am -- I was asking myself whether we could have a late break and then -- but, of course, you might want to consult with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my client is agreeable to having an extended sitting to try and accomplish the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that you finish not later than by quarter to 11.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, first of all, you mentioned that there was water and chocolates being handed out. Was there also bread being handed out by the VRS soldiers to the Bosnian Muslim civilians that were gathered at Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. They must have distributed, fed them, and then killed them afterwards. It was an alleged distribution, told us to go, pass through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I think it would be better -- it is clear that you are emotional under -- going back to what you experienced. At the same time, we'd like to have answers to the specific questions, the question being at this moment: When chocolates and water was distributed, was bread also distributed? Apart from whatever other feelings you may have had, was bread distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answers the question. Mr. Ivetic, could you put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With the help of the Prosecution, I would like to take a look at a video to see if this accurately depicts the incident you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This will be from the Srebrenica trial video, P1147. It will be from the subvideo number 9266, and is the first segment that I identified for the Prosecution going from 23 minutes and 52 seconds to 24 minutes and 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, madam, I'd ask that you view this video and then I'll have a few questions after we complete the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could stop. And we have stopped now at 24 minutes and 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, is this the incident that you have described in paragraph 10 of your Rule 92 ter statement, the encounter that you had with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present there. There were many people when he said that. There were groups of people on the tarmac, on the road, and there was a meadow nearby, but I hadn't gone that far to hear him say that. He probably did, but I wasn't there. He just said that we will go to Alija, but I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what Mr. Ivetic would like to know is what you described as having seen -- being relatively close to Mr. Mladic, whether what you see on the screen is the same moment or is this different, and were you not present here when he spoke these words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no bread being distributed here, no juice, no water, no chocolate, in this footage. Where we were in the meadow, that's what I was talking about. That was before. As for this, I hadn't gone this far. He probably did say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are the words being spoken by General Mladic in this clip consistent with the words as you remember them that you recall General Mladic saying which you did hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has explained that this was not where she was present. Whether it's consistent or not, we have the evidence of the witness, we have this video, and whether there is any consistency or inconsistency is a matter of judgement rather that anything else. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to look at another segment of this same video, and with the help of the Prosecution I would now play the segment from 27 minutes and 19 seconds to 28 minutes and 3 seconds, which should be the second segment that I identified for them. And, madam, again I'd like to have your assistance to watch the video first, and then I'll have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with that we can begin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, madam, do you recognise this incident? Is this perhaps the encounter that you had described in your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, as for what he said, that's not what I heard. You can see how many people there were. But on the -- at the other place, he went into the masses, and probably no one shot any footage there to be able to hear what he told us. He didn't say it to me alone but to everyone else who was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, is it -- am I correct that there were UNPROFOR soldiers as well as a tape barrier separating the refugees from the VRS individuals? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. It is correct. I knew what UNPROFOR looked like. I didn't know what was going on. I couldn't be everywhere, but where I was, there were thousands upon thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you is it your testimony that General Mladic crossed the tape barrier between the refugees and the VRS soldiers and proceeded into the crowd beyond the UNPROFOR soldiers by himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you want to have a clear answers, you should adapt your questions to -- first of all, you are now putting a different question from the previous one, and if you would -- yes. Well, I don't know whether you're interested in hearing an answer of the first question, because there was no clear answer to that. Ms. Osmanovic, could you tell us, did you see at any point in time a red and white tape separating the group you were in from another area? Did you ever see such a tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In all the trauma, I didn't see it, in all that hell. I was sitting -- well, not only he. There were Serb soldiers separating children and men to the left side, and we were just sitting on the buses or the trucks. Some people were left behind. It was all hell for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. I do understand how you felt at the time, but you have not seen a red and white tape separating the group you were in from others. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see it. I only heard in the evening some screams, some hell, some moaning. No one could sleep or anything. I saw people. I knew my neighbours from Bratunac. They were on foot, walking next to me. One of them told me, his name is Salihad, he told me not to be afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Osmanovic, Mr. Ivetic will put his next question to you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there UNPROFOR soldiers separating the crowd of refugees from the VRS soldiers at the time when you encountered General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I only heard General Mladic say that, what I have already explained. He said whatever possessions you had, discard them. The Serb army will come in. I saw him. He said so. Perhaps no one filmed it. And what's the use of me repeating what I saw a dozen times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Osmanovic, I think you've answered the question. Carefully listen to the next question Mr. Ivetic will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did General Mladic enter the crowd of refugees by himself?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I don't know if he was alone or whether there was someone else in all that chaos and hell. I can't recall if he was alone. There were just moments. You don't know. I couldn't understand. They just told me it was Mladic. I didn't know the man. They said, Mladic, Mladic. I can't say that I saw Karadzic or Boris Tadic or Nikolic or this or that when I saw Mladic and I heard him say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, madam, I'd like to look at a -- well, first of all, the two videos that we've already looked at, the demeanour of General Mladic, is it similar to or different from the demeanour of General Mladic during the encounter that you remember with him?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was hell where he said that and when I saw him. I didn't take part in anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Osmanovic, Mr. Ivetic would like to know whether the behaviour of Mr. Mladic as you saw it on your screen a few minutes ago, whether that was similar to when you saw him, whether he was behaving differently or whether it was approximately the same when you saw him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He passed by, and he said what he said. He passed us by. He said so. I don't know. This is better when he said that the children should go to Kladanj in the footage we saw, like he did to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you say he was a bit more friendly on what you saw on the screen compared to what you saw and heard him say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? It is simple for me to watch this now, but there was hell in Srebrenica. I don't know how to explain it or tell you. I can't understand any of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said that General Mladic at that occasion told you to leave your personal belongings. What personal belongings did you leave?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He said that we should discard our things, the Muslim people, whatever we had on them, saying that the Serb army was about to come in. He said so. It can't be that he didn't. He told us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If anyone had anything on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. -- Mrs. Osmanovic. Did you have anything with you which you left after Mr. Mladic had said that you had to leave your belongings? Did you have anything you were carrying with you and left, or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had two photo albums with the pictures of my children. I left them in Potocari. What else could I have? I left my house on the 8th of May and arrived in Srebrenica. I didn't have anything, as a housewife. What could I have? Where is my husband? I was in another person's apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left the albums in Potocari, the pictures of my children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you left them? Did you just drop them on the ground, or were they taken from you, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the ground. On the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question, please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, at temporary transcript page 32, line 1, you said: "He said that we should discard our things, the Muslim people, whatever we had on them, saying that the Serb army was about to come in. He said so. It can't be that he didn't. He told us that." The question I have for you, then, is: Is it your testimony that this individual -- this individual you identify as Mladic came and told this to the people before the Serb army came to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I don't know. I knew some of my neighbours from Bratunac and Hranca and Kalimanici, from Bajina Basta. I knew them, where I was seated. I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, my time is limited. I'd like to look at one more video-clip with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this will be the same video, the segment at 24 minutes and 35 seconds, going through 26 minutes and 56 seconds. And with the help of the Prosecution, if we could play that clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, did you have occasion to hear or learn from the other refugees that a delegation of civilian representatives from Srebrenica asked General Mladic to evacuate the civilian population out of Srebrenica, those that desired to leave? Was that something that was talked about?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I didn't hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A similar question. Did you have occasion to hear other refugees talking about the last part that General Mladic said, that they wished that the resolution to the crisis offered in 1993 had been accepted earlier to peacefully resolve the crisis? Was that something that was talked about?

utterances.speaker: SALIHA OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that, believe me. I don't know. I don't know. I wasn't interested in politics. How would I know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Thank you for answering my questions. Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Ms. MacGregor, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No questions on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Osmanovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague, and the Chamber understands that being taken back to the events in the mid-1990s must be emotional for you. We appreciate that you came and that you have answered all the questions that were put to you, and we wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and thank you for having invited me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to make one comment. I think it's evident that this witness obviously has some confusion about what she remembers from seeing it personally versus what she's seen in the video. The only evidence that she has provided about General Mladic that the Prosecution will be relying on is that evidence that is in her statement at paragraph 10 referring to General Mladic and that testimony that she gave today that is consistent with that statement. And I actually do have transcript references to places where we will not be relying on her comments about the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider how to deal with the evidence given by this witness, and it is on the record that you said the Prosecution will not rely on everything, especially not where the Prosecution thinks that the witness may have observed matters on the video rather than in a live experience. We take a break, and we resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Malagic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you now. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mrs. Malagic, you'll first be examined by Ms. Harbour. Ms. Harbour is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find her to your right. Ms. Harbour, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Malagic. You testified before this Tribunal in the Krstic, Tolimir, and Karadzic cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to listen to your direct examination from the Tolimir case before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions that you were asked in the Tolimir case, would you provide the same information in substance?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The transcript of the witness's direct examination from the Tolimir case is 65 ter 28892, and would now like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question before we proceed. I take it that your testimony in the Tolimir case was to the best of your knowledge in accordance with the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It becomes P1462, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1462 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would now like to read a short summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained to the witness the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Ms. Harbour will now read a summary of what is found in your testimony in the other case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In May 1992, local Serb leaders in Mirsada Malagic's village near Bratunac gave the Muslims an ultimatum that they had to leave. Ms. Malagic and her family fled into the nearby woods. Between 1992 and 1995, she lived in a number of villages in the vicinity of Srebrenica and Potocari. During that time, she and her family suffered from the deprivations inflicted on the refugees living in the enclave. In particular, there was constant shelling in 1992 and into 1993, and there was never enough food to satisfy the needs of the overcrowded city. On 11 July 1995, the witness and her family were compelled to flee Srebrenica. Her husband, two eldest sons, and brother fled into the woods to try to reach Tuzla by foot. Ms. Malagic was injured by shrapnel when the Serb forces shelled around the UNPROFOR camp in Srebrenica. She made her way by foot with her younger son and her father-in-law to Potocari. During the evening of the 11th and the 12th of July, they stayed in the Zinc factory in Potocari. They could hear screaming and moaning from nearby structures. On 13 July, Ms. Malagic saw Mladic speaking to the crowd of refugees in Potocari and assuring them that nothing would happen to anyone. As she made her way with her son and father-in-law to the buses to be evacuated, Serb soldiers separated out her 70-year-old father-in-law along with other men. She and her younger son got on the bus to be evacuated. Ms. Malagic never saw her husband, her two older sons, or her father-in-law again. And this concludes the public summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Harbour. If you have any further questions for the witness, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Ms. Malagic, I'm going to ask you a few questions first about your experiences in the period beginning in 1992. In your prior testimony, you testified about being forced to leave your village of Voljavica and making your way through the woods to Srebrenica. You testified at T 110 [sic] that: "Srebrenica was deserted. Private homes had been torched, looted." When you arrived in Srebrenica and you saw that scene, what impact did that have on you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Srebrenica some 18 days after I had left home in Voljavica, I was very disappointed. It was a very difficult day for me, much more difficult than the moments when I was leaving my home. It was because when you see so many torched houses in Srebrenica, all those private homes, the homes of prominent people alongside two streets were literally torched, and whatever I could hear and see and smell suggested of burning. Occasionally I would see a stray dog, but there was no one else there. It was a desert. All was grey, without people. When you see your own town look like that, because you spend many years working there, I used to work in the mine administration, the deserted town -- well, all I could do was sit down and tears began flowing in front of the cultural hall. And then I realised that we were in a vicious circle with no way out. We couldn't go any further at all sides. In Potocari there were check-points. We couldn't go anywhere. There were Serb soldiers at all of the surrounding places, including Spat and the Zinc mine were in Serbian hands, because that's where we had to leave from. My town or my place of residence was also abandoned because it was blocked, and at that time I began thinking where I brought my children to and why did I come here in the first place. For the first time I was afraid, not knowing how it would all end. There were many incidents, many murders, many tragic incidents that we could see when we were still back in our house. However, there was no way out. We couldn't go back, and even then we were surrounded. Only the Drina was there, which was always a border. We couldn't cross it over into Serbia. Whoever managed to leave before that did, while the other -- the others stayed in the villages. We were one of the first to go down into Srebrenica, which was deserted. Everything was open, the doors to apartments. Houses were burned. So you could take your pick where to find accommodation. We were in an apartment. My second-oldest son had a fever, and we stayed there for a few days. After the initial four to five days, I met with my brothers who survived in Potocari. We then went to their family house, which was still in good condition at the time. I spent the entire summer of 1992 there, and we stayed there until sometime in December 1992, when we had to leave. We were exposed to much shelling at the time, and many shells hit our family home, and we basically moved from one room to the next until we were forced to go down to the garage and had no where else to go. Then my brothers decided that I with my children should go to Srebrenica. We found accommodation there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, sorry to interrupt you for a moment. What Ms. Harbour wanted to hear from you whether -- perhaps not all the details of what you found but, for example, that it made you very depressive to see how the town was almost empty and that so much damage was there. Ms. Harbour, it's up to you to use your time in such a way that you -- and you asked for one hour and a half, which is compared to the previous witness, three times as much. Could I ask you to -- to try to keep tighter control over your examination. Witness, I hope you understand that we hear a lot of evidence from many persons, sometimes very detailed, sometimes with less detail, so Ms. Harbour will indicate to you where she is seeking the details and where the overall impression would at this moment be sufficient to hear of. You may proceed, Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one correction on the transcript. Ms. Harbour, you referred to transcript page 110 of the Tolimir transcript, but it was 10010. Just to correct line 11 of page 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Ms. Malagic, you have answered and anticipated indeed many of my questions. My next question for you is: While you were living in the area of Potocari and Srebrenica in 1992 and 1993, did you or your family ever go hungry?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Practically from day one after we'd left our home we suddenly didn't have any food. So on the third day after our departure, my husband, my two sons, and a couple of relatives had to go back to our home over the night in order to collect any food that they could find because we were already short of food. And that situation continued. We were looking for food by going to our native villages, and we mostly went there during the night, and that was the only source of food that we had because we were unable to carry anything with us when we left home.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Just to give the Chamber an example, was there a period of time in January 1993 when this hunger affected you in a very personal way?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In early January 1993, actually towards the end of December 1992, people were virtually dying of starvation, and myself and my family were in the same position. If you managed to get hold of any food, you would keep that for your children. So as a result of starvation, I fell ill. There was a doctor in Srebrenica who remained, and he didn't flee anywhere, and we asked him for help, and at that worst of all moments he managed to give me four intravenous vitamin injections. I knew him from peacetime. He was an occupational doctor. And he simply told me, "You are hungry. You are starving." He couldn't give me any other medication. He tried to help me recover with those injections. However, after I received the third one on the morning at 9.00, this doctor was killed that same day by a bomb that was dropped from an aeroplane. The bomb hit the mosque. His house was close to the mosque. So as a result he and other residents of Srebrenica who lived nearby were all killed. After that --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. I think that's sufficient to give the Chamber an understanding of what you went through. Can we now fast forward to early 1995 before Srebrenica fell, so around January 1995. Was there enough food to go around in Srebrenica during that period?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. The winter and January of 1995, and especially during the springtime, people had to walk to Zepa to fetch flour, because you were happy even to have a slice of bread. I had a sister in Zepa whom we used to visit, and she offered us some food. They had more food than we did in Srebrenica. I don't know how and why. So we brought this food back and distributed it. We had one meal a day. We divided the bread to our children, one slice each, just in order to survive, and that all went on throughout the spring of 1995. The idea during that spring was to sow any piece of land and soil, every green area that can provide some crops in order for people to survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now turn to the events beginning on July 11th, 1995. In the Tolimir case, you testified that after your family set off together towards Srebrenica -- or towards the Srebrenica UNPROFOR compound, your older brother, husband, and your older sons Elvir and Adnan separated from you to try to reach Tuzla by foot. And this is at transcript page 10014, and 10017 to 18. Where did you say good-bye to them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that was between the UNPROFOR compound and the hospital in Srebrenica near the former petrol station. Let me just correct you. You said Admir and Adnan. Actually, those were Admir and Elvir. Adnan was with me. He was my youngest. We all arrived there together, but as I already said, shells started falling. There was a huge crowd of people. There was commotion. So there was simply no free space. When the first shells fell, there was commotion, and I actually didn't have a chance to say good-bye to my dear ones. We just went our ways. Adnan, my youngest son, and I and my father-in-law thought we would be unable to walk such a long way through the wood, and we decided to go to the UNPROFOR compound instead, whereas they went the other way towards Kutlici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Why did your father-in-law stay with you and your younger son instead of joining the men to go to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: For a simple reason that he was poorly. He was an elderly man. He was 70 years old, and he didn't believe that he would be capable of travelling such a long way and that he would try to seek shelter in the UNPROFOR compound. He believed that women and children would be at least safe in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you take anything with you as you left Srebrenica and went to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we set off, I took with me only one bag with a loaf of bread that I had baked in the evening, and one of my sons also had a bag, but when I was wounded by the shell, I wasn't able of carrying the bag so I had to leave it. And when my son and I arrived in Potocari, we virtually didn't have anything with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You testified previously that on your way to Potocari, an UNPROFOR trucked passed by you, and you saw your eldest son Elvir and his friend in the truck and that they waved at you. And this is at transcript page 10022 of your Tolimir testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'd like to please ask the court officer to bring up Exhibit P1137, and we'll focus on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Ms. Malagic, a witness who was at the Potocari UNPROFOR compound testified that the document which will come up on our screen was a list that they made of the male population in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995, a list which they later gave to DutchBat. And that's transcript page 9893 in this case. Now, we have page 4 or -- in front of us. Do you recognise your son Elvir's information on this page?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under number 22, Malagic, Elvir. Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You testified previously that on the morning of 13 July 1995, you heard General Mladic speaking, telling people that nothing was going to happen to anyone. And this is transcript page 10034 of your Tolimir testimony. Can I ask you, who was Mladic speaking to when he said this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, there was a huge crowd of people there. I didn't have a watch at the time, so I can't tell you when was that, but all of a sudden, after the night of the 12th of July, everybody wanted to leave Potocari. Everything that they experienced during the night, including myself, forced those people to hurry up. A few went outside into the street. There was so many people there. It was enormously hot. There were many people. There was a huge crowd. So it wasn't possible for everyone to come close to the place where the Serbian soldiers and General Mladic came. Anyway, when they and he addressed the crowd, and the crowd was standing, I think that was within the compound of the former slaughterhouse, and next to it is the Srebrenica transport company, and there was a barricade nearby that we later crossed over to board the buses. Anyway, he addressed this crowd of women, men, and children closest to him had, but since there were so many people, we weren't all able to be nearby, but a promise was made that enough buses would be provided for evacuation, that nobody would come into harm's way, that we shouldn't be afraid. So in response, the people closest by applauded. Probably at that point in time they believed that that would be true, but it seems that this was only for the cameras, and nothing that happened later was even remotely close to what we had expected. And when we arrived at the barricade, nobody from Potocari was able to cross over.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Was Mladic in Potocari on the 12th of July as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Although I couldn't see him then. I was within the Zinc company compound, but my sister was there. She was seeing off her daughters when a promise was made that women with babies would be evacuated first. She had a baby with her, and General Mladic and the Serbian Army arrived from Bratunac. Then I saw buses and trucks, but they were far away. I wasn't able to see who they belonged to until the next day when I crossed over the barricade and boarded it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: So your sister told you that she had seen General Mladic on the 12th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we return for a moment to the men in your family who fled into the woods from Srebrenica toward Tuzla. You told the Court in the Tolimir case that on the 11th of July, your younger brother went toward Potocari for food, and later your older brother, your husband, and your sons went on foot into the woods. And this was at transcript page 10014 in that case. Did your younger brother manage to reunite with the group that headed into the woods, and that is with your older brother and your husband and your sons?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They reunited in Buljim, I think, or any of the villages up there, and from there they proceeded towards Tuzla all together.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did your brother survive the journey all the way to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both my younger and elder brothers were lucky enough to reach what we believed was the free territory, but when they came across the first ambush at Kamenica, they separated and they lost sight of each other and nobody was with anyone else any longer. Only in Nezuci, after having exited from the woods, did my brothers reunite, whereas my husband and my sons never appeared again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: After you were evacuated from Potocari, what did you do to try to find your husband and your sons Admir and Elvir?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
