utterances.text: Well, the first people who emerged from the woods were driven to Zivinice. That was actually a field or a point where they were brought on board buses and trucks. I tried to go there and locate anyone. However, in that first group I didn't see my brothers either because they were not there. They found a brother-in-law of one of my brothers who was in Tuzla, and they drove him to his father in Banovici, because my younger brother was unable to walk any longer. They had to carry him to the nearby medical centre for treatment. Only after a few days when he recovered a little they managed to locate me, because I was staying in a school in Zivinice where I was brought from the Tuzla airport, and that is where I reunited with my brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You told us in your prior testimony that you were never able to reunite with your husband or your sons. What was it like for you not knowing where they were, your husband and your sons?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a great shock. I looked at every man arriving there, but when you set off there but you had a kind of premonition that the one you're waiting for would not be there. However, when I saw my brothers, I was happy to see them survive, but I was equally shocked and disappointed, and I had some bad premonition that something terrible had happened to them and that they would never appear again. Despite that, I was hopeful during those days that they might appear, that they were alive, and this is what kept me going with my life, this kind of anticipation and expectation, but with every day that passed, it became weaker and weaker, and we know what was eventually confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In the Tolimir case, at transcript 10040 of that case, you told the Chamber that your father-in-law, your husband, and your middle son Admir had been found and buried. Do you know where their remains were found?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. My father-in-law was found in a grave in Snagovo near Zvornik. It's all Zvornik municipality. And my husband and my middle son Admir were found at Zvornicka Kamenica. A year later, my elder son Admir [as interpreted] was also found in Zvornicka Kamenica, and he was buried on the 11th of July of 2012, and we buried my husband and my middle son in November 2010, which was 15 years after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, you just referred to your eldest son Elvir -- or Admir. That was actually Elvir; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have only a few more questions for you today. During your testimony in the Krstic case, you told the Chamber about a statue or a monument that you saw while you were walking around The Hague, and you told the Chamber about its significance to you. Now, before we talk about what that statue meant to you, could you just describe what that statue was and where it was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: When I came in 2000 to testify in the Krstic case, we had some time so we took a walk around the town. I was in a hotel at the beach, and I didn't know the city too well. However, we came across a statue, and this statue has woken something in me. It is a woman glaring, and of course since I didn't know the language, I asked the woman who took us for a walk what was written on the monument and what it represented. She told us that that was a monument to the fishermen who were killed, that there were so many of them who killed -- who were killed that their wives and sisters were waiting for them for years and years, but none of the fishermen returned because there were lots of shipwrecks and other accidents. I saw myself in the statue of that woman who had such a lost sight on her face. I didn't know either what was the destiny of my husband and my sons and other relatives. And I wanted to try and find to buy a small copy of this statue, because I thought that we were comparable, because we were both gazing, only I was gazing through this huge forest in which all our husbands, sons, and other men disappeared. And this sentiment that emerged within me gave me hope to keep waiting. However, in 2009, I received a first report from the centre in Tuzla that the remains of my husband had been found. A few months later, I received a report that my middle son Elvir was found. I had to go and identify them, and we buried them, as I said, in 2010, on the 15th anniversary of the fall of Srebrenica. Then in 2011, I received another invitation to come and identify my oldest son. When I buried him at the memorial centre in Potocari, that was the time when I buried my last hope with me. All my close relatives, my entire family, was under the ground. I had no hope whatsoever. There was no one that I could wait for. The truth had come out, and it became apparent that I'm really alone. And I'm still cherishing this statue that I bought in this city which I have visited for a fourth time this time. I'm sorry that it had to be in that way, and I would like to thank everyone who gave me an opportunity to come here, to tell me what I think and how I feel, and to just give a piece of the truth that all my fellow countrywomen had experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Harbour. Ms. Malagic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic, you'll find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, madam. I deeply regret the loss you have suffered and which cannot be compensated for. Given the fact that we come from the same part of the world and speak the same language, I just wanted to ask you to briefly pause between question and answer so that we could have it all in the transcript. I will not have many questions for you. I would kindly ask you to tell us the following: When you mentioned in your examination-in-chief that you left your village of Voljavica, please tell the Court when it happened, to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, 1992, at 7.30 p.m. That's when I left my home and my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber the following, please: To the best of your knowledge, what kind of unit was it, what kind of people they were to give you such an order to move out?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I can't really say, or perhaps I won't be able to express myself the best way in terms of what kind of unit it was. We had our people, our representatives in the local commune. The adjacent settlement of Pobrdje, towards Bratunac, comprised the same local commune as Voljavica. Our delegates who went there to talk to them -- and before that check-points had already been erected at Pobrdje, and we couldn't go to Bratunac. The people in question wore camouflage uniforms. We didn't know who they belonged to. We didn't know them. We only received representatives from that local commune in the course of those days. They also came before while we were being disarmed. We knew those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to be more direct in my questions. Is it correct that one of those people who came and whom you remember regarding disarmament and the taking away of weapons from your villages was Miladin Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also accurate that you remember him from that time as someone who had worked in the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you for another clarification, please, concerning your life in Srebrenica between 1993 and 1995. Tell the Court who was it who went to fetch food in Zepa from Srebrenica, from your household?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: From Srebrenica to Zepa, my husband went as well as my older son. Of course they never went all together. They changed, since it was a long way to travel. Both my brothers went, too, and during that last winter -- actually, not the last one but the winter of 1993, or between 1992 and 1993, it was my older brother who went, and he had trouble along the road because his feet froze. There was much snow. He was brought back from Zepa since he couldn't walk back alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard them describe the passage between Srebrenica and Zepa. Was it unhindered, and did they have to go through VRS-controlled territory which was outside the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't travel that route. I don't know the route, but I do know they had to be accompanied by someone who did. I had a son-in-law who hailed from Zepa --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He knew what route to take, and they mostly travelled at night. I don't know what places they went through along the route, though, because I never covered the distance on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly that your sister lived in Zepa itself or in a village nearby?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: She lived in Zepa at the time. However, before the war she used to live in Glodjani, which was 20 kilometres from Han Pijesak. However, the village had been torched and she fled to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your years in Srebrenica, was your husband engaged militarily?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war all of us, that is to say, all of our men, were engaged, if you can call it that, because they stood some kind of guard along the separation lines. Whichever village we came to, everyone saw us as refugees, and as such one had to be on duty, without weapons or anything, and I claim that positively. Given the fact that at the very beginning of the war, that is to say, less than two months after we left home, my husband's brother was killed. In late 1992, another brother of his was killed when looking for food. And after that, no one tried to force my husband to go, because he was the only person alive from the family. So he only went to search for food. He went down to the Drina, to Voljavica, and in the direction of Pavkovici because there was a field there and they gathered corn under -- from underneath the snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were his brothers registered as the shaheed and were their families as the Sehid families taken care of?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: The families of both of them, that is to say, their wives and children left Bratunac before the war. One of the wives was a refugee in Slovenia, and she's currently in the Netherlands, whereas their son was killed during the attack on Srebrenica. As for the younger ones, they had left Slovenia and they're also now in the Netherlands, so they were not there in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the two men, were they killed as the shaheed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to answer that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can't, please say so.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question, because as I said, they were killed at the very beginning the war, especially the younger brother-in-law was killed by an air bomb, carrying a sack of corn on his back. So he wasn't in any military operation. He was literally gathering corn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the plight of the Serb civilians, Serb population in the valley of the Drina, in Skelani, and in Kravica, in 1992 and 1993? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't. Between 1992 and 1993, as I explain to the Court, I was very ill and was bed-ridden at home. My husband was with me, and he didn't go to Kravica. And my children, of course, were there. We were simply trying to stay alive at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was cautioned that the term "shaheed" made its way into the transcript. Since we come from the same part of the world, can you confirm that in B/C/S it could be interpreted as "soldier," or is there another term to explain the word "shaheed"?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify. You could answer that one way or another. In my mind, that is incorrect. My brother-in-law --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My father-in-law, who was 70 at the time, according to the documentation in this unfortunate Bosnia-Herzegovina war of ours, is treated as the shaheed. If a 70-year-old person was a soldier, then I have to ask myself who can be a soldier or a shaheed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please: Were you ever informed by your late husband what unit he belonged to and where he stood the guard you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: The initial guard duty occurred in the villages of -- in the village of Brezovica, before we even reached Srebrenica. Later when we moved to Potocari, then they stood guard at Likari and Caus. If you come from that area, you know what I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you what unit it was and who was his commander?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I know that in Srebrenica it was said -- and that even after Srebrenica fell, people referred to it as the 20th Division. They called it that, and that's all I know about those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 1993 and 1995, did you know that many people, due to the situation in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica, wanted to leave the area and go to Tuzla or Sarajevo, or perhaps some other destinations controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I knew, it took place that spring of 1995. So as late as 1995. That's when I heard some people say that they wanted to leave Srebrenica and that something terrible will happen and that one had to leave Srebrenica in any case. I know that people wanted to leave, and I know of some groups that took to the forest. They must have used some routes in order to reach Tuzla. Some of them got through, although I don't know by what route. Others were perhaps killed and, for the most part, all traces lost of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about your family and you during the period between 1993 and 1995? Were you looking for a way to leave the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apologies. Do you know that there were inhabitants in the enclave who went in the direction of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I only heard about that, but I don't know anything. I heard some stories of some people going to Zepa and then trying to cross over from there into Serbia or further afield. I don't know such routes, and they were only stories. I'd rather not say they were correct or incorrect. It's only something I heard from other people. There were always a lot of people around, and one could always hear stories. However, it is not reliable information that I could confirm as true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will conclude before the break with just one more question. In the period between 1993 and 1995, was the black market in operation, and were food articles and cigarettes as well as fuel being smuggled in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: As I said already, I don't know if it was because we were too honest or too ignorant, my family and I didn't know about that. We didn't have money to buy things with, and we had no other sources of supply. I knew that people went to Zepa and brought coffee and salt. So one could buy that. None of us smoked, so we didn't even think about cigarettes. At the market in Srebrenica, which barely functioned, one could buy things. For example, a kilogramme of salt cost 70 German marks, and I could only dream of that. I didn't have any kind of money at the time. So for three years we went on barefoot, thirsty, and hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You hail from the area of Potocari; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your brothers' and your family home is in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, from 1993 to 1995, when the enclave -- once the enclave was established, your brothers lived in the area of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. Only in 1992. Until late 1992, we lived together in Potocari. Then I went to Srebrenica as I said. And they, too, had to leave, perhaps a month after me, before General Morillon entered Srebrenica. There was a guided missile of sorts, although I'm not familiar with weapons, but I know that their house was demolished and they had to go to Srebrenica where they lived in an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did that apartment belong to that they lived in before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly slow down and pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited to slow down and to make pauses between question and answer. The witness has answered your last question that she doesn't know to whom the apartment belonged. Mr. Stojanovic, I'm thinking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will conclude with this question before the break, which I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the apartment where you lived belonged to before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a house just behind the cultural hall owned by the municipality. A man used to live there who worked in Banja Guber in Srebrenica. He was a Muslim in that house where I lived in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please turn the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Switch on your microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is a good time for our break, and after it I will move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you give us an indication as to how much time you'd need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. According to our plan, it will be shorter than envisaged, and we will conclude in the one hour that we have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd say in the next session, within one hour you would conclude, which also means that there's some time left, Ms. Harbour, although limited time, for questions in re-examination. We'll take a break, but could first the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I would like now to move on to the events of the 11th, 12th, and 13th of July, 1995. I'm going to ask you if it is true that already on the 10th of July, you were outside the UN compound in Srebrenica because you wanted to know how and which way you would go.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were told to go back home, and the night between the 10th and 11th, you spent in the flat where you were living at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, you went again in front of the UNPROFOR base in Srebrenica, and that is when you set off towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who specifically told you to go to Potocari? Whose idea was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, at first this whole crowd of people - I wasn't alone there - spent maybe one or two hours, I don't know, I didn't have a watch, within the UNPROFOR compound in Srebrenica or what used to be the old workshop as it was known. We were not able to communicate with them due to the language barrier. Some people were climbing on the trucks, because women with children believed that they would be evacuated. It was total commotion. It was too hot. The area was packed with people. At one point we heard the sound of aircraft, and that is when two Dutch soldiers, I don't know who they were, showed us with their hands towards Potocari, because we couldn't communicate verbally, and they also pointed at the aircraft trying to reassure us not to be afraid, because as far as we were able to understand, bombing was -- was going to happen, or air-strike. That's how I understood them. Anyway, they showed us into the direction of Potocari with their arms, which we understood that we should go towards Potocari. Nobody told us specifically that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the bombing on the 11th -- or, rather, the flights of aircraft, were you able to see -- or you were not able to see the Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer, because there was no pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. The question was whether you were able when the -- the aircraft were flying over, whether you were able to see or not able to see the Serbian Army at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question was: At that point on the 11th of July, was your late husband and your sons already on the way in a different direction, as you put it, towards the woods?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. When we headed towards the UNPROFOR base, they took the road towards Susnjari and Kutlici and the other villages. I don't know what happened after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you have any information at all who told them to head for Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information at all at that period that able-bodied men should head towards Jaglic and Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any direct or indirect knowledge of the fact that both the civilian and military authorities of Srebrenica had requested a couple of days before the 11th to enable the civilian population of Srebrenica to leave, and that happened during negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did it take to cover that way between the UNPROFOR base in Srebrenica to the industrial complex in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, time-wise I cannot give you an exact answer. I might be mistaken, but the distance is about 4 kilometres. So if you take an average man, it will be possible to walk, but the situation was that there was a huge crowd of women with children, elderly people, and I said that there were even wounded people among them, myself included. We walked along this asphalt road, but I don't know how long it took us to reach Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, to the best of your estimate, what time in the afternoon it was on the 11th of July, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we may have arrived in Potocari at around 4.00 in the afternoon or 4.30 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at one intersection before Potocari, if viewed from the direction of Srebrenica, members of the BH Army were directing able-bodied men to take this side road to the left to Jaglic and Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any of that while I was on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, did you see General Mladic after you spent one or two nights in Potocari? Please try to remember.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: That first night between the 10th and 11th of July, and in the morning on the 12th of July, as I described, the Serbian soldiers entered Potocari. That means on the 12th of July. After that, given that I had been wounded, I wasn't able to move around a lot. I don't know what time it was. Maybe it was 11.00 or 12.00. Anyway, at around noon, I'm not sure, I already said that my sister came, and she told me that the Serbian soldiers had come from the direction of Bratunac and that Ratko Mladic was with them. Because I was surrounded by thousands of people, I wasn't able to see that section that she was describing, but as I said, it was from the direction of Bratunac. I wasn't in the street at all at the time. I was on the plateau within the compound of the Zinc factory with other people. People were saying and shouting, but I personally wasn't close enough to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, can you be sure that you spent one or two nights in Potocari before you saw General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Sir, the second night in Potocari was chaotic. I personally believe, and I believe that even if you or anyone else was there -- wouldn't be able to remember even what your name was in view of what was happening during that night and that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. That is why I'm asking you. Let me try to go step-by-step. Do you remember that at one point, and I would say that that was on the 20th of July, 1995, which means shortly after you arrived in Zivinice, you gave a statement to the state commission for the collection of facts about these events?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that occasion you mentioned the date or the time when you saw General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: One of those days when he used to say that the women and children and other men would be safe, that everybody would be evacuated wherever they wanted to go, if they wanted to go, and that is what General Mladic said personally in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just stop you for a while with this question: When General Mladic was saying these things, did you personally have an opportunity to see and hear?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I was [Realtime transcript read in error "wasn't"] able to hear him, but I wasn't able to see him because I was not near enough.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I was able to hear him, but I wasn't able to see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. There's a correction. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We are waiting for the record to be completed. Do you recall that at any point you heard or saw this statement of General Mladic being filmed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to hear from anyone that his statement was recorded on camera?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, at the risk of creating further confusion, still the correction of the interpreter leads to a confusing transcript. The last thing I heard is that the witness told us that she was able to hear Mr. Mladic, but she was not able to see him. Witness, that is what you said, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in the course of the two days that you spent in Potocari, bread and water in limited quantities were distributed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the situation the same on both days, the first and the second day that you spent in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: On the second day, the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, can you give us an estimate of the time when you managed to board the vehicle that you mentioned and to head for Tisca and Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what time it was, but I think it was at around noon or maybe one hour in the afternoon, but it was a sunny day. It was very hot, and judging by the position of the sun, I think it may have been at 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon when we boarded the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what members of the UNPROFOR were doing during this whole process?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: You mean while we were boarding the buses?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Both before and during the process of your boarding the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, during the entire time that we spent in Potocari, I was on the road in front of the factory called the 11th of March where I used to work. There was an APC parked there when we arrived in Potocari, but actually after we already arrived, the UNPROFOR soldiers returned us from the barricade. It was not a barricade. It was a tape that was stretched, and they made a motion with their hands that we should go back because there was no room left for any more refugees. So my father-in-law and my child and I decided to go back to one of those factories. Then I saw a soldier tied to an APC, and there was a soldier lying on the APC, but I didn't know what was happening, in fact, but in the days that followed, I cannot tell you exactly at what time, I was able to see the soldier taking off his uniform and giving it to a Serb soldier. I don't know if he was forced to do that or what. Now, having seen these images, I realised that these people can do little for our sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Did you at any point in time receive any food, water, or medication from UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, not in the part where I was. I didn't see that. Perhaps in the perimeter covered by UNPROFOR something like that may have happened, but not on the street or in the factory building where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether at any point in time between the place where you were and the place where you entered the vehicle you had to go between UNPROFOR vehicles which were funneling you towards your vehicle along the road?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. There were masses of people moving at the same time as I was trying to move down the street from the Zinc factory to the transport to Srebrenica on the right-hand side. There was a lot of crowd, and you couldn't see anything from the people. They were all trying at once to go to the tape and reach the trucks and buses where they were told they would be transported. People were in panic and afraid, and they all wanted to leave at that same moment to go through this -- this so-called barricade as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that it was summertime and given the number of people, it was simply impossible for them to remain in the area. Would that be correct? There was a threat of epidemic and people going hungry or thirsty.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, when the temperature rises up to 40 degrees, when you have to spend three days in a row out in the open, because I managed to find a spot on the bus after three days, and I can only discuss my feelings, but never at any point in time did I, my son, or father-in-law think of anything else. We didn't take any water, food, or medication that the Serb soldiers may have distributed. We only took sips of water from time to time at a gas station nearby, and that's how we survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony in a previous case, you mentioned two people whom you had known from before, Gavric and a policeman that you referred to regarding 1992. Do you recall that part of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court where you saw Gavric, and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I saw Milisav Gavric at the gate of the 11th of March factory and the Zinc factory. So there was a single fence and a single gate through which one could go to both factories. He was there in the afternoon of the 12th of July. He was standing with a group of people, including my husband's uncle. There were also three brothers from Potocari whom I knew and a man from Tegari who drove a taxi in Bratunac in peacetime. There was a conversation of theirs, although I didn't stay since I was on my way to get water. I saw them, but I couldn't hear what they were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the process of population evacuation, as people were getting aboard buses and men were being separated, were there any military or policemen there? Did you ever find anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think there were any police, in my view. The person I mentioned a moment ago, Jokic, I saw him on the 13th of July en route to the buses. He wasn't there, and he wasn't along the road before the barricade in Srebrenica. He was just standing by the road, kept to himself. He didn't talk to anyone. He wore a light blue shirt and grey pants. I think it was a police uniform. As for the other people who were there as we were getting onto the buses and trucks, when the men were being separated at the barricade, they were all in combat fatigues, in military uniform. Now, who those people were, who they belonged to, whether they were the Serb army from Republika Srpska or something else is something we couldn't tell. In any case, they were young, and I've already stated that such young people could have been soldiers. Judging by their accent and conversations, one could conclude they were from Serbia, because they only spoke the Ekavian dialect that no one in Bosnia speaks. It was easy to notice that. As I was getting some water, I heard a couple of them even say that they were from Valjevo. And they also had camouflage uniforms. I don't know whether they said the truth, though, but that's what I could hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But they, too, spoke to the Ekavian dialect?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, please: During the two days in Potocari, did you at any point in time receive information that there was a delegation of the refugee population which participated in discussions with the political, military, and police leadership concerning the evacuation of those people? Did you ever obtain such information?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us whether the following names mean anything to you: Camila Purkovic, Nesib Mandzic, and Ibro Nuhanovic. And did you know those people from earlier, from before?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew the first person. She worked in Srebrenica when I worked there, in peacetime. I knew Nesib Mandzic from the war. I think he was the principal of the school during the truce period. As for Nuhanovic, he was an UNPROFOR interpreter, as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told that an agreement was reached with the Serb authorities and UNPROFOR to have the people evacuated from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told at any point in time that during that evacuation UNPROFOR members were to take place as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to look at some footage taken on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at P1147. It is V000-9267. I would kindly ask Janet to show us the other clip beginning at 5:46 to 6:30. 5:46, and then 6:30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and thank you, Janet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you could observe, madam, it was on the 13th of July, slightly after the time you provided as the moment of your departure from Potocari, the Serb policeman or soldier, which happens to be irrelevant for this case, is addressing an UNPROFOR soldier and tells the interpreter the following: "Miki, tell them to go and collect them from up there. Miki, they should tour the area to see if anyone else wants to go. That's their job." Having heard this and seen the footage, let me ask you this: Did you at any point in time have information that UNPROFOR members were supposed to take part in organising the evacuation of the people from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's look at another footage from the same recording. It is P1147, video V000-9267, starting with 3 minutes and ending at 4 minutes, 26 seconds. Let's have a look at it, madam, and then I'll have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose you were able to see this footage on several occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what we have received from the Prosecution, it is supposed to be the 13th of July, early in the afternoon. Given the place of your birth, do you recognise the part of Potocari where this was shot?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Sir, I know Potocari as the back of my hand. As for all this footage, they cover the distance between the 11th of March and the UNPROFOR base and the Zinc and battery factory. We were all put on the vehicles with which we were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you to clarify the following: In this -- on this footage, in this column, you could see men, women, the elderly, and younger men and women as well with their personal possessions, packages. Where was this part recorded?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I know that beyond the UNPROFOR barricade -- that's what I can say. Well, when we reach the barricade, when we were seated, that group of people, that crowd that accompanied us was seated across the road. On the left-hand side there was the so-called white house, and before that house was the barricade. On the right-hand side was the Feros factory and the old slaughterhouse. When we went beyond the barricade we turned right to get on the buses, and all of the men, all of the men, every single one, my brother-in-law, my father-in-law, et cetera, were told to go to the left and told that they would be put on some other buses. They were escorted across the canal to the house. They threw their back-packs next to the road. I don't know what they were told, but I could see that. And the people were then taken to the house. Where they were taken later is something I don't know. By that time we had already got on the buses, and the people stayed in the yard of the house and behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time observe whether the same kind of procedure was followed on your first day in Potocari, that is to say, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you saw it, tell us whether these people, as you could see on the footage, could bring along their possessions on the trucks and into the buses.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. According to what others told me, because I didn't see it, but according to the stories of others later on, those who were there on the 13th in the morning, and this may well be the time of the footage, although I'm not sure, we were told that there were some older men who managed to get through. That is to say, they were not separated, and that they could bring along their possessions. When my group came along, we were told literally to throw it away, that we wouldn't need it, that beds awaited us, and that we were to go to our Alija and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of the men who managed to pass the barricade, as you said, discard their passport or any other identification document?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. All I saw that they were throwing away their rucksacks or bags or whatever they had but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You already spoke about the next thing that I'm going to ask you about and testified more extensively in the previous cases. Do you remember when the convoy of vehicles with the refugees was passing through Bratunac that the local population was hurling threats at them, swearing at them, that one could feel hatred among the people in the street aimed at you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the same situation repeat itself while you were passing through Milici?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if that happened while you were passing through Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: When I was passing through Vlasenica, the bus stopped at one point. We didn't know what was going on. The bus had a flat tire, and while we were parked there nobody approached us except for three men. I don't know who and what they were. One of them entered through the door and gave three apples which were not ripe yet to a child sitting next by, but they did nothing else. Once the tire was repaired, we continued our journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers in the vehicles or outside the vehicles? And I'm referring to members of the UNPROFOR escorting the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a long convoy, and there was no one in front of our bus, but I don't know whether there were soldiers anywhere else, because as I said, that was a long column. There was no escort in front or behind our bus. I told you that in three places we had to stop. The buses were boarded by Serb soldiers who were asking us to give them foreign exchange currency, otherwise they would kill us. Some of the women did give their money, and they stopped us again at Kravica and then again. And when the third time they tried to stop us, the driver said, "People, we are being stopped for a third time. The people have nothing more to give you."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At what time were you stopped at Kravica, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Kravica is not far away. I don't know how long it took when we started from Potocari and reached Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you would agree that it was on the afternoon of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, having in mind everything that you experienced during your journey, were you able to conclude that the people in Bratunac were extremely vengeful?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you remember when you arrived beyond Tisca and when you got off the vehicles and started walking towards Kladanj that you saw an UNPROFOR vehicle there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any vehicle there. When we got off, I saw soldiers on both sides of the road who were directing us and telling us not to deviate from the road. Those people who were exhausted and old and frail had to be carried, but we were all exhausted for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We are nearing the end, but before that, I'd like to call up 1D84 in e-court. It's an excerpt from the book entitled "Chaos by Design," written by Ibran Mustafic. We're going to look at one passage from the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need the next page in the document, the last paragraph in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting let me ask you this: Do you know who Ibran Mustafic is?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we have a good habit in this court that we first explore whether the witness has any knowledge of something the party would then like to show to that witness. So I don't know what is in the book, or whatever, but first ask the witness about what you want to show her later and to ask her whether she's familiar with any of it, because there's no need to show it if she don't know anything about it. So would you please proceed in accordance with this guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will comply, Your Honours, and I think I started with asking the witness who Ibran Mustafic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you this: Is it true that he was a delegate in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war and that he represented the Party of Democratic Action? Are you familiar with that information?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I heard that he had been a deputy in the Assembly, but I don't know. I didn't know anything about the authorities, but I heard that he was the deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in those days he himself was in Potocari too?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see him in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read this very characteristic passage, and I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you first should inquire with the witness whether the witness has any knowledge on the subject you want to deal with, and only if she says she knows something about it, then it's worthwhile to put a text to the witness. Perhaps it might not even be needed if the witness knows a lot and can tell you a lot about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this guideline, and I'm going to abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, let me ask you this: Do you know that in the course of the separation of able-bodied men in Potocari, at any location or at any check-point or in the course of any segment of the process Camila, Nesib Mandzic, and Nuhanovic were present?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of these three individuals on the 13th of July in the vicinity of the place where the able-bodied men were separated?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, in light of this, I don't think it is necessary to put this document to the witness. It is still in e-court as 1D.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to conclude my cross-examination by asking you this, madam: After all these tragic events, did you go back to live in the place where you lived before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to a decision issued by the Department for Refugees and Displaced Persons, was your property restituted in your former place of residence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to repair your property, at least in part?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have to slow down. Did you receive any subsidies in that respect that helped you to repair your property?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You and your family are now living outside Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a registered residence in Bratunac, and in the last elections, did you have an opportunity to be on the electoral roll for Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you exercise your voting rights?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo -- or, rather, Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the population of your village return to their properties where they used to live before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam. I have no further questions for you. Once again, I'm very sorry if I put any question to you that would invoke the memories that you have of these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, do you have any -- is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench also has no questions for you, Madam Malagic, I would like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties. The Chamber is aware that it is not easy to be taken back to the events which happened in July 1995. The Chamber is fully aware of that. Therefore, thanks again, and we wish you a safe return home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would take this opportunity to thank you, this Trial Chamber, and the Hague Tribunal in general, and this country that made it possible for us to give at least a partial account of what really happened to us, in order to describe a situation that my family and thousands of other people found themselves, people who lost their property, their families, their children, people who were left alone, deprived of any will to continue with their lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were called in order to assist the Chamber in finding the truth. Thank you again very much. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need to take a break because there are no -- any further witnesses, so therefore before we adjourn, I'd like to briefly put two matters on the record. First, the Defence requested, on the 13th of May, 18 days to respond to the Prosecution's 26th 92 bis motion which would extend the deadline for a response to tomorrow, the 17th of May. The request is hereby granted. Second, I'd like to put on the record -- rather, the Chamber notes that as of the 1st of June, 2013, the Chamber will be sitting five days per week pending a decision, the decision on the Defence motion for an adjustment of the trial sitting schedule. These were the two matters I wanted to put on the record. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the Chamber's last comment about the sitting five days, given the scheduling implications, the Prosecution certainly would appreciate any notice as soon as possible if that is going to change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is at this moment considering the Defence motion for adjustment of the trial sitting schedule and as soon as we have decided or whether that will be a final decision or any interlocutory decision, of course you'll know it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, during the testimony of Witness Zlatan Celanovic at transcript page 11109, the Chamber inquired about what appeared to be a transcription error in the witness's testimony in the Popovic case, which was tendered in this case as P1451. The Chamber pointed out a sentence which occurs in the original text at transcript page 6635, and at e-court page 11, line 23, in the transcript which reads: "I did thought mention the 28th Division, and I didn't know where there was a 28th Division." The Prosecution has checked the corresponding B/C/S audiotape of the transcript, and informs the Chamber that the English translation in our view would correctly read: "I did not mention the 28th Division, and I didn't know there was a 28th Division." I don't know whether the Chamber and the Defence are willing to rely on the representation of the Prosecution and we leave the matter there, or whether the Chamber wants to direct that the matter be checked by somebody else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Defence would agree that this is how we should understand the transcript of the testimony and that there's an error and that the parties agree on what the error is and how it should correctly be read, then the Chamber would like to hear from the parties and may finally not ask for any further steps as long as the parties agree on the matter. At least the logic is back in this sentence. Whether it's accurate or not, that's a second matter, but it's, again, logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that that is the case, but since my colleague Lukic led this witness, and I wouldn't like to become involved in this issue, I'd prefer to have an agreement with the Prosecution that we verify this, and we shall inform you shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber hear from the parties within seven days from now. Then we adjourn for the day. We will not sit tomorrow, and therefore we will resume on Tuesday, the 21st of May, at 9.30 in the morning, and to be quite honest, I do not know whether it will be in Courtroom I or Courtroom III. It will still be in Courtroom III. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of May, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
